stories.title: Let's Encrypt is adding two additional remote perspectives for domain validation
stories.author: gslin

topComments.author: throw0101a
topComments.text: In August an attacker was able to get a certificate issued even with multi-perspective validation: > For 33 hours in late August, a rival network hijacked a block of Hetzner-hosted infrastructure serving Softaculous and Virtualizor, using it to issue a valid TLS certificate and push a malicious software update. The stolen route was RPKI-invalid the entire time, on file, checkable by anyone. It still won on most of the internet. > At 20:57 UTC on 28 August, a network nobody at Hetzner or Softaculous had dealt with before started announcing 162.55.80.0/24 to the internet. It was a small, unremarkable-looking slice of Hetzner’s own address space — the block hosting Softaculous’s client area, its billing pages, and the update endpoint that every Virtualizor-licensed control panel on the internet periodically calls home to. For the next 33 hours, with an 11-hour lull in the middle, a meaningful share of global traffic bound for that block went to the hijacker instead. Some of it was Let’s Encrypt’s own domain-control validation, which is how the attacker walked away with a certificate for virtualizor.com that no browser would ever flag. * https://cloudpunk.blog/post/bgp-hijack-rpki-gap/ So it's all very well to have multiple network locations to prevent hijacking on the path (i.e., you have to attack multiple paths), but if the network as a whole thinks the destination is someplace else then all those paths will lead to the same (false) location. Perhaps the CAB should consider RPKI validation as a "MUST" rather than piling on multiple sources of validation who still have the same single point of failure (the spoofing of the destination).

topComments.author: Schlagbohrer

topComments.author: nbadg
topComments.text: For anyone else who didn't have "remote perspectives" in their personal technical lexicon: this refers to performing the ACME challenge/response check when validating the domain of a certificate signing request from multiple physical locations, and therefore via multiple physical network routes, in order to make network-level attacks more difficult. For example, if you were validating example.com, you'd need to set up some response to the ACME challenge somewhere, either through direct DNS-based validation (DNS-01, DNS-PERSIST-01) or through a server running at the resolved A/AAAA IP address for example.com (HTTP-01, TLS-ALPN-01). In all cases, when a CA goes to validate your challenge response, it relies both upon DNS and upon the network integrity between the CA's datacenters and your DNS and/or app servers. Both of these can be subverted, eg via BGP attack, to allow an attacker to replace a DNS response, re-route the destination IP address to a different server, etc, at which point they can inject their own challenge response, and therefore issue their own (unauthorized) certificates. Multi-perspective validation means that the CA validates your challenge response from multiple datacenters on different networks instead of just one, such that a hypothetical network attack would have to target multiple independent networks in order to successfully issue their unauthorized certificate. More info: https://letsencrypt.org/2020/02/19/multi-perspective-validat... https://community.letsencrypt.org/t/multi-perspective-valida...

jobs.text: I’m Chris, VP Engineering at Fazeshift. We’re nine engineers plus our Founder/CTO and me, and I’m hiring someone who can help us do more, better: increase both what we can build and the quality and sophistication of the software we build. Accounts receivable sounds boring until you look under the hood. It sits at the intersection of money, business relationships, software systems of various vintages, and a huge amount of repetitive human work. Instead of giving finance teams another dashboard to stare at, we’re building AI agents that actually do the work across billing, collections, payments, cash application, and the systems connecting them. We’ve grown revenue 12x since 2024, and eight unicorns now run AR on Fazeshift. A big part of what makes the engineering interesting is that we’re intentionally not the system of record. Our customers already run on ERPs, CRMs, banks, billing systems, payment processors, spreadsheets, and internal software, so we have to understand state across systems we don’t control, act safely in them, and recover when reality disagrees with what an API says should have happened. A timeout doesn’t necessarily mean a write failed. Webhooks can arrive late or twice. A payment may not contain enough information to identify an invoice. In those cases, blindly retrying can be exactly the wrong thing to do. We use coding agents heavily ourselves. Engineers use Conductor, stacked PRs, Linear, and multiple frontier models every day, with internal skills and tooling that let agents drive and validate our local development environment. We’re especially interested in engineers whose development workflow has already materially changed because of coding agents: people who are comfortable delegating meaningful work, keeping independent threads moving in parallel, debugging where agents get stuck, and improving the surrounding system when the workflow breaks down. But generated code is still your code . Judgment, debugging, systems thinking, taste, and understanding what actually shipped matter more here, not less. Our development style is roughly: design enough to find the shape of the problem, then build to learn. There’s a short distance here between noticing a problem, deciding what should happen, building it, and seeing the result in production with our customers. You’ll own meaningful problems from ambiguity through design, implementation, rollout, and production, and you’ll work directly with the people affected by what you build. We’re looking for 5+ years of professional experience, strong TypeScript/full-stack skills, solid systems judgment, and real production ownership. No fintech background needed. Stack: TypeScript/Next.js, tRPC, Prisma/MySQL/PlanetScale, Inngest, AWS. I read every HN application myself. Email chris.zehner@fazeshift.com with HN in the subject, your LinkedIn/GitHub/résumé, and a few sentences about something interesting you’ve built or improved recently.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Android WebView dropping cookie / not setting cookie
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I have a web application that handles a login flow from a guest link in two steps: We process a request to /auth/guest-link?auth=<token> ; this request, on success, returns a 307 Temporary Redirect, with a Set-Cookie header that contains a session cookie. The next page looks for the Cookie header, to find the session token. This works well enough on desktop, and on mobile when the link is entered directly into the URL bar in Firefox. However, when I send the link over Discord, and click the link in Discord, it opens in that weird not-my-browser thing; I think the technical term for it is Android WebView, but I'm not certain¹ (I'll call it the "mini-browser" henceforth). When that occurs, the following happens: /auth/guest-link is successful. It returns a 307 Redirect & Set-Cookie header, normally. The next request from this mini-browser does not send the Cookie header at all. The cookie is SameSite=Strict , and when I relax that parameter (by removing it) for the purposes of debugging, then the flow succeeds, and this mini-browser sends the cookie normally on the second request. Note that we're not changing domains or origins, or going from http:// to https:// ; both requests are https:// , both requests are to the same domain name. The exact cookie construction (this in a Rust actix-web app) is: let cookie = Cookie::build("session", session_token) .secure(true) .http_only(true) //.same_site(actix_web::cookie::SameSite::Strict) .path("/") .finish(); Is there something I'm doing wrong here? Is this just a bug in the Android mini-browser that it doesn't respect SameSite=Strict ? Edit: I've now connect to this "mini-browser" via Firefox's about:debugging tools. (So, it is definitely Firefox.) I can thus inspect the page with DevTools. infoqArticles.title: Pinterest Uses Event Time Watermarks to Finalize Petabyte Scale Data Partitions
infoqArticles.description: Pinterest has introduced event time-based partition finalization for its database ingestion framework. The mechanism uses Apache Flink to track event time and Apache Iceberg metadata to publish a non-regressing watermark, helping downstream jobs determine when continuously ingested CDC data is sufficiently complete for processing. By Leela Kumili
infoqArticles.author: Leela Kumili

infoqArticles.title: JEP 543 Finalizes Structured Concurrency in JDK 28, Ending Seven Preview Rounds
infoqArticles.description: JDK 28 finalizes structured concurrency through JEP 543, with no API changes from JDK 27. Teams on JDK 27 only need to drop --enable-preview and recompile. Code written for JDK 25 or 26 must adapt to the R_X exception type parameter, ExecutionException wrapping, and the abstract timeout() joiner callback. By A N M Bazlur Rahman
infoqArticles.author: A N M Bazlur Rahman

infoqArticles.title: Article: From Microservices to Agents: The Next Evolution of Distributed Systems
infoqArticles.description: The article examines the transition from microservices to agentic AI architecture in distributed systems. Microservices allow for functional decomposition, while agentic systems focus on decision decomposition. This shift introduces new complexities in observability, reliability, and system design, highlighting the need for updated architectural patterns and practices. By Mallika Rao
infoqArticles.author: Mallika Rao

infoqArticles.title: Podcast: The Future of Web Apps: Will AI Agents Generate UIs on the Fly?
infoqArticles.description: Rachel Lee Nabors, former React core team member, dives into the architecture and philosophy behind local-first applications, exploring how small language models (SLMs) running directly on-device can deliver privacy-focused, low-latency, and cost-effective alternatives to cloud-hosted LLM wrappers. By Rachel Lee Nabors
infoqArticles.author: Rachel Lee Nabors

infoqArticles.title: EmbeddingGemma 2 Expands Beyond Text to Support Code, Images, Video, and Audio
infoqArticles.description: Based on Gemma 4 and released under the Apache 2.0 license, Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 is a compact, open-weight, multimodal embedding model designed to make semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) more efficient while optimizing performance for on-device deployment. By Sergio De Simone
infoqArticles.author: Sergio De Simone

infoqArticles.title: Buildkite Adds Scoped Secrets and New Agentic CI Tools
infoqArticles.description: Continuous integration provider Buildkite has introduced pipeline-scoped secrets and new Model Context Protocol tools for validating pipelines, diagnosing failed builds and repairing webhooks. The company has also added Linux arm64 support to its GitHub Actions compatibility layer and expanded OpenTelemetry data in Buildkite Agent v4.1.0. By Matt Saunders
infoqArticles.author: Matt Saunders

infoqArticles.title: .NET 11 Release Candidate 2: Go-Live License and Updates Across Libraries, F#, MAUI, and WinForms
infoqArticles.description: Microsoft has released .NET 11 Release Candidate 2 under a go-live license, supported in Visual Studio 2026 Insiders. The release adds incremental CBOR reading, experimental post-quantum cryptography APIs, file-based app directive improvements, NuGet package cooldowns, F# runtime async building blocks, a C# UI option for .NET MAUI, and refined Windows Forms visual styles. By Almir Vuk
infoqArticles.author: Almir Vuk

infoqArticles.title: NestJS 12: ESM Packages, Standard Schema Validation and Native Observability
infoqArticles.description: NestJS version 12 has been released, transitioning core packages to ESM and adding Standard Schema validation. It updates the CLI and introduces an observability SDK. Key changes include project generation choices between CJS and ESM, improved validation options, and lifecycle project hooks. Users will need Node.js 20.19+ or 22.12+. Migration guides are available for upgrading. By Daniel Curtis
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Curtis

infoqArticles.title: Google Adopts Pyrefly for Faster, More Accurate Python Type Checking
infoqArticles.description: Google has replaced its long-standing Python type checker, Pytype, with Pyrefly, an open-source tool originally developed by Meta. The decision was driven by Pyrefly's advantages, including faster and more accurate type checking, and lower infrastructure costs. By Sergio De Simone
infoqArticles.author: Sergio De Simone

infoqArticles.title: AWS Introduces Preview of Well-Architected Agent
infoqArticles.description: AWS recently announced the preview of the Well-Architected Agent, a service that analyzes environments against Well-Architected best practices and provides prioritized recommendations across cost, security, performance, and reliability. The AI agent can also suggest remediation steps and review infrastructure-as-code before deployment. By Renato Losio
infoqArticles.author: Renato Losio

infoqArticles.title: AWS Will Run Its European Sovereign Cloud Without the Global Backbone for Several Hours
infoqArticles.description: On October 24, AWS will operate its European Sovereign Cloud without a connection to the AWS Global Network backbone, with a team of EU residents and the region’s own hardware and software. AWS says neither of the two systems being severed is operation-critical, and practitioners are divided over whether the exercise answers the question customers are asking. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
infoqArticles.author: Steef-Jan Wiggers

infoqArticles.title: Reverse Engineer Anything Project Brings AI Agents to Binary Analysis
infoqArticles.description: Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) is an open-source project with over 200K GitHub stars that connects coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex to reverse-engineering tools like Ghidra, Hopper, and IDA. The project lets developers inspect compiled binaries, trace function calls, and investigate how applications implement specific features. By Renato Losio
infoqArticles.author: Renato Losio

infoqArticles.title: Amazon Acquires DuckLabs and Integrates DuckDB in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL
infoqArticles.description: Amazon has acquired DuckLabs, the company behind the analytical database DuckDB. Co-founders Hannes Mühleisen and Mark Raasveldt will continue to lead the team under AWS. The acquisition aims to enhance the development and reach of DuckDB while maintaining its open-source status. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL gets its first DuckDB-powered feature following the acquisition. By Gianmarco Nalin
infoqArticles.author: Gianmarco Nalin

infoqArticles.title: Google EnvHarness Enables Self-Evolving Agents to Learn in Dynamics Environments
infoqArticles.description: Google researchers open sourced EnvHarness, a framework that dynamically adapts agent-training environments to an agent's weaknesses without modifying the agent, environment, or evaluation system. According to the researchers, this approach can improve both learning effectiveness and efficiency while helping agents overcome their weaknesses. By Sergio De Simone
infoqArticles.author: Sergio De Simone

infoqArticles.title: Zod Brings In-Process Schema Compilation and a 9x Cut in Memory Footprint
infoqArticles.description: Zod is a TypeScript-focused schema validation library that recently released versions 4.5 and 4.6. Key updates include schema compilation for faster data parsing, significant memory usage reductions, and new validation features. The library supports efficient validation processes and remains popular in the JavaScript ecosystem, achieving millions of downloads weekly. By Daniel Curtis
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Curtis
